📚 DAILY MARKET EDUCATION
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

1. LEVERAGE: Free vs Used Margin
- Understanding your account balance metrics is critical when trading volatile commodity markets like crude oil or gold
- Used margin is the portion of your capital locked by your broker to keep your open positions active
- Free margin is the remaining equity available in your account to open new positions or absorb floating losses
- Real Market Example: If you buy a standard contract of Brent Crude Oil and your broker requires one thousand dollars in margin, that becomes your used margin. Any remaining equity in your account is your free margin to trade other assets like natural gas.
- Practical Tip: Always monitor your free margin level during high-impact news releases to avoid unexpected stop outs on open commodity trades.
SMART MONEY RULE: Never let your free margin drop below fifty percent of your total equity during choppy market sessions.

2. TERMINOLOGY: Rollover & Swap Rates
- Rollover and swap rates are the interest adjustments applied when you hold leveraged trading positions overnight past the daily market close time
- Depending on the interest rate differential between the underlying assets and the direction of your trade, you may pay a fee or earn a credit
- Real Market Example: Holding a leveraged buy position in spot Gold over the weekend incurs swap charges because you are effectively financing the purchase through your broker.
- Practical Tip: Check your broker specification table for triple swap days, which usually occur on Wednesdays for most commodity and forex instruments.
PRO TIP: Intraday traders should close positions before the daily settlement time to completely avoid holding overnight swap costs.

3. DAILY TRADING TIPS
- Respect the daily range: Commodities like Silver and Natural Gas often experience sharp mean-reversion moves after breaking initial session highs or lows.
- Watch inventory reports: Always check economic calendars for weekly crude oil inventories and natural gas storage data before entering directional trades.
- Protect your capital: Friday sessions often bring unexpected profit-taking flows, so tighten your stop losses on all open commodity positions heading into the weekend close.

4. RISK MANAGEMENT: Risk-Reward Ratios
- A risk-reward ratio compares the distance between your entry price and your stop loss against the distance to your profit target
- Maintaining a positive risk-reward ratio ensures your winning trades generate more profit than your losing trades cost you
- Real Market Example: If you risk one hundred dollars on a Gold breakout trade to make three hundred dollars at your target, your risk-reward ratio is one to three.
- Practical Tip: Avoid taking commodity setups where the required stop loss is wider than your logical profit target.
PRO TIP: You can maintain profitability with a win rate below forty percent if you consistently execute trades with a minimum risk-reward ratio of one to two point five.
